Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Amir, a 37-year-old firefighter, sits stiffly in the chair, his broad shoulders held in a tight, protective posture. For six months, his world has been shrinking, a process that began with a man on a bicycle. The man had been a neighbor in his old apartment complex, and the stalking started subtly: a figure always at the edge of his vision when he went for a run in the park, the same bicycle leaning against a wall near his favorite coffee shop. It escalated over two months, from unsettling coincidences to the undeniable feeling of being tracked. The man would appear on his bicycle at the end of Amir’s street, just watching. The ordeal culminated one evening when Amir returned from a long shift to find the man waiting by his front door, a confrontation that ended with a restraining order but left an indelible mark on Amir’s sense of safety in the world.

The initial relief that followed the legal intervention was short-lived. Now, any bicycle can undo him. A few weeks ago, while driving to the station, a cyclist in his peripheral vision sent a jolt of pure ice through his veins. The world seemed to tilt, and for a moment, he wasn't on the highway but back on his old street, the memory returning not as a thought but as a full-body certainty of imminent harm. The wave of emotion was so powerful, so overwhelming, that he had to pull over onto the shoulder, gasping for air until the feeling subsided. He can no longer drive past his old neighborhood, and the park he once loved is now a no-go zone. The feeling of being followed is a constant companion; the sound of footsteps behind him on a grocery store aisle is enough to make his heart hammer against his ribs.

At the fire station, a place once synonymous with control and competence, Amir feels like an imposter. The sudden, jarring clang of the station alarm, a sound he has heard thousands of times, now makes him flinch violently. He finds himself constantly on high alert, his eyes darting to the bay doors, watching anyone who approaches the building with a suspicion that feels alien to him. Even in the familiar breakroom, he reflexively scans for exits the moment he enters, a habit he cannot seem to break. He watches his crewmates, men he trusts with his life, searching their faces for any sign of a threat, knowing on some level it’s irrational but unable to stop the internal surveillance. This constant vigilance is exhausting, and it has not gone unnoticed. His captain recently commented on his jumpiness, a remark that felt like a confirmation of his deepest fear: that he is fundamentally broken.

He has come to believe that the man he was before the stalking is gone forever, replaced by this fragile, terrified stranger. He is convinced he has been permanently changed for the worse. The intensity of his reactions—the panic attacks in the car, the constant state of dread—has planted a terrifying seed of doubt in his mind: he fears he is going crazy. As a firefighter, his identity is built on strength and the ability to run toward danger. Now, he feels like the weakest person he knows, and this chasm between who he is supposed to be and who he feels he is has become a source of profound shame. When his wife, Layla, asks him what’s wrong after she finds him staring blankly at a wall, he is paralyzed. He knows precisely what happened, the images are seared into his mind, but he is unable to find the words to describe the experience. The memory is a locked box of pure feeling, and language is a key he cannot find.

This inability to articulate his experience has built a wall between him and Layla. He has stopped trying to explain, certain she would think less of him, or worse, confirm his fear that he is losing his mind. It was after a particularly bad night, when the sight of a pizza delivery cyclist on their street sent him into a silent, shaking panic, that Layla finally gave him an ultimatum filled with more fear than anger. She told him she felt like she was living with a ghost and that she couldn't watch him disappear anymore. That was what brought him to therapy. He is here not with hope, but with a quiet dread, terrified that putting words to his experience will only prove that the damage is permanent and that the strong man he once was is truly gone for good.
